findings.headline: Monitoring Officer function resourcing reviewed due to increasing governance demands, complaint volume and LGR work
findings.detail: The Council has reviewed the resourcing of the Monitoring Officer function "in light of increasing governance activities, volume of complaints, and the work involved in providing governance advice connected with Local Government Reorganisation". The statutory Monitoring Officer functions are currently "undertaken by a small team". An action for 2026-27 is to review whether the function has "sufficient resources to carry out statutory function alongside the additional, specialist governance advice that will be required alongside the LGR process".
findings.matters: The Monitoring Officer is a statutory post with specific legal duties. If under-resourced, governance may suffer or the council may face risk of unmet statutory obligations. The review acknowledges this as a concern.
findings.figures: No specific staffing numbers provided; described as "small team"
findings.quote: The resourcing of the Monitoring Officer function is an area that has been reviewed in light of increasing governance activities, volume of complaints, and the work involved in providing governance advice connected with Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: No Monitoring Officer Section 5 reports issued in 2025-26, a change from prior years' breaches on UASC matters
findings.detail: The Monitoring Officer did not issue any Section 5 reports under the Local Government and Housing Act 1989 during 2025-26. The paper notes this is "in contrast to earlier years, where there were a number of Section 5 reports presented in connection with breaches of statutory duties arising from Kent County Council's involvement in judicial review proceedings relating to the care of unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC)".
findings.matters: Section 5 reports indicate the council has breached statutory duties. The absence of such reports, particularly given prior years' issues on UASC care, suggests resolution or improved control of those specific risks. This is positive governance news compared to the prior situation.
findings.figures: Zero Section 5 reports issued in 2025-26
findings.quote: The Monitoring Officer, during the period of this Audit up to the time of writing, has not issued a Notice pursuant to s. 5 of the Local Government and Housing Act 1989.

findings.headline: Implementation of agreed audit management actions improved to 61-64% in 2025-26 from 34% in 2023-24
findings.detail: The rate at which the council implements agreed management actions to address audit findings has risen substantially. In 2023-24 it was 34%; by 2024-25 it had reached 62%; in 2025-26 it was 64% (January) and 61% (July). The paper describes this as "a positive step" to be "built upon in 2026-27".
findings.matters: Implementation rates show whether the council acts on its own audit findings. Improving rates suggest the council is disciplined in addressing identified control weaknesses. This is a positive governance trend.
findings.quote: In 2024-25, full implementation rates increased to 62% in 2024-25 from 34% in 2023-24. The positive trend in implementation of agreed management actions was taken into 2025-26 with implementation reported to January (64%) and July (61%) Governance and Audit Committees.

findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion of Adequate Assurance maintained since 2019-20, but with increased Limited assurance areas
findings.detail: Internal Audit assigns "Adequate Assurance" to corporate governance, risk management and internal control overall. This opinion is consistent with ratings since 2019-20. However, the proportion of systems/processes assigned "Limited" assurance increased to 17% in 2025-26 from 15% in 2024-25. Positively, 50% of systems received "Substantial" or "High" assurance (maintained from prior year).
findings.matters: Adequate assurance is the middle of the assurance scale. The increase in Limited assurance areas warrants monitoring. The maintained Substantial/High rate is positive. Finance directors track audit opinion trends as indicators of control effectiveness.
findings.figures: Adequate assurance overall; 50% Substantial/High (unchanged); 17% Limited (up from 15%); maintained since 2019-20
findings.quote: Internal Audit concludes that Adequate Assurance can be assigned in relation to the Council's corporate governance, risk management and internal control arrangements... There has been a maintained trajectory in the proportion of systems, processes or functions which are assigned an assurance level of "Substantial" or "High" with 50% in 2025-26 in line with 50% in 2024-25... There was a slight increase in the assigning of "Limited" assurance in 2025-26 to 17% from 15% in 2024-25.

findings.headline: Government paused Local Government Reorganisation on 7 September 2026 after announcing 4-unitary option on 16 July
findings.detail: The Government initially decided on 16 July 2026 to proceed with Option 4B (four new unitary authorities for Kent and Medway), with shadow elections planned for May 2027 and vesting day 1 April 2028. However, on 7 September 2026, the Government announced a review of the LGR programme and confirmed plans for Kent and Medway would be "paused". The paper describes the scale, complexity and timing of LGR requirements as "already having, and will continue to have, a significant impact on the operating position and capacity of the Council".
findings.matters: LGR creates major organisational uncertainty. A pause after months of preparation is costly in terms of staff distraction, planning resources, and creates new risks. Lenders need to know about major structural uncertainty affecting the council's future direction and stability.
findings.figures: Option 4B announced 16 July 2026; pause announced 7 September 2026; shadow elections were to be May 2027; vesting day 1 April 2028
findings.quote: On 16 July 2026, the Government announced its decision to proceed with Option 4B for Kent and Medway, which would establish four new unitary councils... However, on 7th September 2026 the Government announced a review of its Local Government Reorganisation programme and confirmed that plans for Kent and Medway will be "paused" while that review is carried out.

findings.headline: Late engagement with governance processes continuing to place strain on statutory procedures, creating ongoing operational risk
findings.detail: The review found that "late engagement with governance processes, often driven by political timetables, external dependencies or capacity constraints" remains "a continuing risk". The paper notes that "decisions taken close to deadlines increase pressure on statutory processes". Officers also reported that Members and the public may not fully appreciate "the shrinking capacity of the service directorates".
findings.matters: If the council cannot complete governance processes on time, statutory decision-making is at risk and quality of decisions may suffer. This is particularly concerning given the significant financial challenges requiring careful financial governance. Finance directors watch whether councils maintain governance standards under pressure.
findings.figures: No specific figures; described as ongoing/continuing risk
findings.quote: In particular, late engagement with governance processes, often driven by political timetables, external dependencies or capacity constraints, was recognised as a continuing risk. While compliance with internal governance remains high, decisions taken close to deadlines increase pressure on statutory processes.

findings.headline: Isolated but repeated incidents of poor Member behaviour flagged as emerging cultural risk to governance capacity
findings.detail: The review found that "almost one quarter" of governance officers experienced "isolated but repeated incidents of poor behaviour involving specific Members". The paper describes this as "an emerging cultural risk which, if not addressed, could impact long-term governance capacity". It is not considered a systemic issue but a concern requiring attention.
findings.matters: If governance capacity is consumed managing conduct issues rather than enabling effective decisions, the council's operational effectiveness suffers. Lenders and peer councils need to know if the council's internal environment is conducive to effective decision-making.
findings.figures: ~25% of governance officers reporting such incidents with specific members
findings.quote: With a significant minority (almost one quarter) of governance officers experiencing isolated but repeated incidents of poor behaviour involving specific Members... these results present an emerging cultural risk which, if not addressed, could impact long-term governance capacity.

findings.headline: Code of Conduct complaints received 85 times in 11 months, approximately four times the prior year rate, with 40% Member-to-Member
findings.detail: Between May 2025 and March 2026, the Council received 85 Code of Conduct complaints. The paper states this is "approximately four times the amount of complaints received in the same period the previous year". Of the 85 complaints, 40% were Member-against-Member complaints. The paper describes this as "high compared to previous years" and reflects changed political dynamics following the May 2025 change of administration.
findings.matters: A four-fold spike in conduct complaints, especially Member-to-Member, indicates governance stress and deteriorating professional standards. It may signal increased political friction. The paper identifies this as an "emerging cultural risk" requiring continued monitoring. Finance directors care about governance stability.
findings.figures: 85 complaints (May 2025-March 2026); ~4 times prior year rate; 40% Member-to-Member
findings.quote: In total, 85 Code of Conduct complaints were received between 6 May 2025 to 31 March 2026. This is approximately four times the amount of complaints received in the same period the previous year.

findings.headline: Oracle Cloud Programme requires additional £7,562,446 to complete Phase 2 implementation
findings.detail: Phase 1 of the Oracle Cloud Programme (Finance and Procurement replacement) was implemented in August 2025. Phase 2 (HR and Payroll replacement) is in final testing with expected go-live in 2026-27. Additional funding of £7,562,446 is required to complete the full implementation, to be funded from flexible use of capital receipts.
findings.matters: Transformation programme cost overruns are material to councils' financial position. The additional £7.5m reduces available capital receipts for other investment. Finance directors watch how peers manage large IT transformation costs and whether programmes deliver within budget.
findings.figures: £7,562,446 additional funding required
findings.quote: Additional funding of £7,562,446 is required to complete the implementation of the Oracle Cloud Programme. This will be funded from the flexible use of capital receipts.

findings.headline: Spending controls and recruitment freeze introduced December 2025 in response to forecast overspend
findings.detail: In response to the Q3 forecast overspend of £43.5m, the Council introduced "firmer spending controls" in December 2025. All discretionary spending was stopped and a recruitment freeze was implemented immediately. The recruitment freeze was lifted in April 2026, approximately four months later.
findings.matters: Crisis-mode spending controls indicate financial distress. Their introduction shows the council faced a real spending emergency. The timing and duration (December to April) indicate sustained pressure. Lenders care about whether councils can maintain spending discipline.
findings.figures: Introduced December 2025, lifted April 2026
findings.quote: In response to the forecast overspend on the revenue budget, a decision was made to introduce firmer spending controls in December 2025; these were in place for the remainder of the financial year. Under these controls, all discretionary spending was stopped and a recruitment freeze was put into place immediately. The freeze was lifted in April 2026.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £42.9m due to rising demand, complexity and unachieved savings
findings.detail: Within the overall £22.7m revenue overspend, Adult Social Care & Health was the primary driver, with a £42.9m overspend. The paper attributes this to "rising demand, complexity and unachieved savings". This is described as a "substantial pressure" that "again" faced such challenges, suggesting a continuing structural issue.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand pressures are not unique to Kent but how a council manages them indicates whether budget planning is realistic and whether demand is being controlled. A £42.9m overspend in a single service area signals structural imbalance between resources and need. Other councils and lenders watch how peers manage this pressure.
findings.figures: £42.9m overspend
findings.quote: Adult Social Care & Health again faced substantial pressures due to rising demand, complexity and unachieved savings, resulting in an overspend of £42.9m.

findings.headline: Revenue overspend of £22.7m in 2025-26 following £43.5m forecast in Q3
findings.detail: The Q3 2025-26 revenue forecast showed an overspend of £43.5m (2.8% of budget). The final outturn was £22.7m excluding schools. This followed the introduction of spending controls and recruitment freeze in December 2025 to manage the overspend. The paper describes this as "another challenging financial year".
findings.matters: Two consecutive years of significant overspends suggest structural budget challenges rather than one-off pressures. The fact that spending controls had to be introduced indicates the council faced financial distress. Finance directors elsewhere watch how peers manage demand pressures and control spending.
findings.figures: £22.7m (2025-26 outturn), £43.5m (Q3 forecast)
findings.quote: The 2025-26 outturn highlighted another challenging financial year, with a revenue overspend of £22.7m (excluding schools) and a £33.0m overspend in Schools' Delegated Budgets.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grown to £130.5m and identified as the Council's most significant financial risk
findings.detail: The paper explicitly identifies the Dedicated Schools Grant deficit at £130.5m as "the Council's most significant financial risk". This represents cumulative overspends in delegated school budgets that the council carries as a liability. The continuing growth of this deficit is highlighted as a major financial risk.
findings.matters: A £130.5m accumulated liability is material. Finance directors at other councils and lenders need to know about major long-term liabilities accumulating, as they affect the council's financial sustainability and may constrain future borrowing or spending.
findings.quote: The continuing growth of the Dedicated Schools deficit, now at £130.5m, remains the Council's most significant financial risk.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Audit opinion: unqualified opinion expected on financial statements and pension fund in surplus at 104% funding level
findings.detail: The auditor expects to issue an unqualified opinion on the Council's financial statements shortly after the Governance and Audit Committee meeting. Draft financial statements were of good standard and no adjustments were made following audit. The Pension Fund's 2025 actuarial valuation reported an improved funding position of 104% (2022: 102%), with the Fund remaining in surplus. Pension governance arrangements are appropriate.
findings.matters: A clean audit opinion is the baseline. The pension fund in surplus is positive context and reduces one category of financial risk.
findings.figures: Unqualified audit opinion expected; Pension Fund 104% funded (2022: 102%)
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the Council's financial statements. The 2025 actuarial valuation reported an improved funding position of 104% (2022: 102%), with the Fund remaining in surplus.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Governance and Audit Committee effectiveness requires strengthening; 85 member conduct complaints in 2025/26 with 40% member-on-member
findings.detail: The auditor identified a significant weakness in governance arrangements, particularly Governance and Audit Committee effectiveness. The Committee conducted a self-assessment identifying actions needed. The auditor found 'opportunities for further member development, alongside the strengthening of member-to-member and member-to-officer cohesion.' The Standards Committee report (April 2026) recorded 85 member complaints in 2025/26; the report notes 'a significant proportion of the complaints received were by members against other members which indicates member cohesion could be improved.' The draft 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement also references this trend as 'a shift in the political dynamic.' A 2023/24 governance review identified 22 recommendations; the current audit found that 'some of the underlying issues have not been fully resolved.'
findings.matters: Member cohesion directly affects control environment and decision-making quality. A finance director is concerned because poor governance increases the risk that budget decisions, savings plans, and financial controls will be compromised by political dysfunction.
findings.figures: 85 member conduct complaints in 2025/26; ~40% member-on-member; 2023/24 governance review had 22 recommendations, issues persist
findings.quote: In April 2026 it considered a report on formal complaints received under the Member Conduct. The report set out that 85 member complaints have been received during 2025/26 with the vast majority been closed or resolved without the need for formal investigation. The report notes a significant proportion of the complaints received were by members against other members which indicates member cohesion could be improved.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows budget gap of £86.4m for 2027/28–2028/29 assuming zero Council Tax increase
findings.detail: The MTFP approved in February 2026 identified a cumulative budget gap of £96.3m over 2027/28 to 2028/29. The Council has subsequently informed the auditor this has reduced to £86.4m (£54.4m in 2027/28 and £32.0m in 2028/29). However, this assumes zero increase in Council Tax. The auditor explicitly states: 'Future decisions on local taxation, together with the Council's ability to deliver approved savings and maintain expenditure within budgeted levels, particularly in ASCH and CYPE, will be key determinants of its future financial position.'
findings.matters: The Council faces a structural deficit over the medium term. The gap assumes no Council Tax rise; any constraint on taxation would enlarge it. The ability to close it depends entirely on delivering social care savings that have repeatedly slipped.
findings.figures: Budget gap £86.4m for 2027/28–2028/29 (£54.4m + £32.0m); assumes 0% Council Tax increase
findings.quote: The MTFP approved in February 2026 identified a cumulative budget gap of £96.3m over the period 2027/28 to 2028/29. The Council has subsequently informed us that this forecast gap has reduced to £86.4m (£54.4m 2027/28 and £32.0m 2028/29). However, this assumes no increase in Council Tax during the MTFP period.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Q1 2026/27 forecast already shows £21.4m net overspend, mirroring prior year pattern with ASCH £9.1m and CYPE £13.0m overspends
findings.detail: Within months of closing 2025/26 with a £21.6m overspend, the Council's high-level Q1 2026/27 forecast indicates a net overspend of £21.4m. This is primarily attributable to continued pressures within social care: ASCH projected £9.1m overspend and Children, Young People and Education projected £13.0m overspend. The auditor notes this early forecast 'highlights the continuing volatility and financial risk associated with the Council's social care budgets.'
findings.matters: This is not a one-off or a solved problem. Within a quarter, the Council is tracking toward a repeat of the prior year's overspend despite this being a known issue and focus of remedial action.
findings.figures: Q1 2026/27 forecast: £21.4m net overspend; ASCH £9.1m; CYPE £13.0m
findings.quote: The Council has informed us that its high-level Quarter 1 forecast for 2026/27 indicates a net overspend of £21.4m. This forecast is primarily attributable to continued pressures within social care services, including a projected overspend of £9.1m in ASCH and £13.0m in Children, Young People and Education (CYPE). This early forecast highlights the continuing volatility and financial risk associated with the Council's social care budgets.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Oracle Cloud Programme cost has risen to £43.9m (from original business case of £15m), completion delayed to February 2027, with additional £7.5m funding approved July 2026
findings.detail: The Council commenced the Oracle Cloud Programme on 1 June 2023 to replace outdated corporate systems. Original business case was £15m. Phase 1 completed in August 2025, but Phase 2 (HR and Payroll) encountered delays and overspends. In July 2026, the Policy and Resources Committee approved additional funding of £7.5m. Oracle costs now reach £43.9m with revised completion date of February 2027. The auditor notes budget monitoring reports were not always sufficiently clear in demonstrating accelerating costs and risks. A lessons learned review has been commissioned.
findings.matters: Programme cost has nearly tripled while timescale has extended. This signals either poor initial business case or control weaknesses in delivery. Finance directors need to understand whether this is a Canterbury Tale (complex modernization always costs more) or controllable failure.
findings.figures: Original budget £15m, now £43.9m; additional £7.5m approved July 2026; Phase 1 August 2025, revised completion February 2027
findings.quote: In July 2026, the Policy and Resources Committee approved additional project funding of £7.5m required to complete the implementation of the Oracle Cloud Programme. Oracle Cloud Programme costs now reach £43.9m with a revised project completion date of February 2027.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Adult Social Care delivered only 67% of planned savings (£41.9m of £62.6m target); £20.7m slippage contributed to overall overspend
findings.detail: The Council was required to deliver £121.5m of savings across 2025/26 but achieved only £98.6m (81% of target). ASCH achieved only £41.9m against a target of £62.6m (67% delivery), with slippage of £20.7m. Internal Audit issued a limited assurance report on ASCH savings governance, identifying recommendations for improving savings identification, reporting metrics, and lessons learnt. The auditor notes this provides 'further evidence that the arrangements for savings delivery in ASCH were not optimal during 2025/26.' In 2026/27, the ASCH savings requirement remains substantial at £41.7m, but Q1 forecast already shows £4.4m unable to be delivered.
findings.matters: A council relying on savings to offset overspending must have confidence in delivery capability. Repeated failure to deliver ASCH savings while ASCH continues to overspend signals a fundamental mismatch between planned and achievable reductions.
findings.figures: £98.6m of £121.5m achieved (81%); ASCH £41.9m of £62.6m target (67%); £20.7m ASCH slippage; Q1 2026/27 £4.4m ASCH savings unachievable
findings.quote: The Council's 2025/26 outturn report identified that the Council delivered £98.6m (81%) of savings against a total savings requirement of £121.5m. However, in 2025/26, the majority of all savings slippage related to ASCH. In 2025/26 ASCH delivered £41.9m (67%) savings against a target of £62.6m. Savings slippage of £20.7m contributed to the overall ASCH overspend.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Council chose 3.99% Council Tax increase in 2026/27 against permitted maximum of 4.99%, creating £31.8m cumulative revenue shortfall across MTFP
findings.detail: For 2026/27, the Council was permitted to increase Council Tax by up to 4.99% without triggering a referendum. It elected to increase by 3.99%. Budget papers transparently noted this decision creates financial risk, particularly given the Council's history of overspending and reserve erosion. The Section 25 Assurance Statement warned that the decision to raise Council Tax below the permitted level 'poses a long-term financial risk as a result of the Council Tax income forgone', identifying a £31.8m cumulative impact across the MTFP period due to foregone revenue in 2026/27 alone.
findings.matters: This is an explicit strategic choice with quantified downside: the Council accepted financial risk to hold down Council Tax. Finance directors elsewhere need to know how this played out, and whether the operational savings targets that must compensate for the £31.8m shortfall are being delivered.
findings.figures: 3.99% increase chosen vs 4.99% permitted; £31.8m cumulative foregone revenue in 2026/27 across MTFP
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the Council was permitted to increase Council Tax by up to 4.99% without triggering a referendum. However, it elected to increase Council Tax by 3.99%. Budget papers transparently acknowledged the financial risks associated with not utilising the full flexibility available, particularly given the Council's recent history of overspending and reserve erosion. The Section 25 report identifies that the decision to raise the Council Tax charge below the level permitted 'poses a long-term financial risk as a result of the Council Tax income forgone'. The report identifies a £31.8m cumulative impact across the MTFP due to foregone Council Tax revenue in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £130.5m and is forecast to grow to £247.1m over next two years unless SEND Reform Plan mitigates it
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs Block overspent by £64.6m in 2025/26, creating cumulative deficit of £130.5m as at 31 March 2026. This is forecast to grow to £109.5m in 2026/27 and £137.6m in 2027/28 — a total forecast addition of £247.1m. The statutory override that permits holding the deficit as a negative reserve ends on 31 March 2028. The Council has submitted a SEND Reform Plan to DfE; if approved, the Council would be eligible for 90% grant funding of the historic deficit as at 31 March 2026, but forecast 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits remain unresolved. The auditor identifies this as significant financial risk.
findings.matters: When the statutory override ends on 31 March 2028, these deficits will impact the general fund directly. The Council does not have sufficient working balances to absorb them. This represents a potential crisis point for a lender or peer council.
findings.figures: £130.5m cumulative deficit at 31 March 2026; forecast £109.5m (2026/27) and £137.6m (2027/28); statutory override ends 31 March 2028
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Council's cumulative DSG deficit had increased to £130.5m and is forecast to continue growing during 2026/27 and 2027/28. The Council does not have sufficient working balances to support such deficits once the statutory override ends on 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Interim Auditors Annual Report - Kent County Council 2025 2026 - For Committee
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of overspending: Council reported net revenue overspend of £21.6m in 2025/26, driven by Adult Social Care overspend of £42.9m
findings.detail: The Council overspent by £21.6m, representing 1.4% adverse variance against original budget of £1,531.9m. Adult Social Care and Health reported an overspend of £42.9m (6.1%). This marks the fourth consecutive year of overspending (prior years: 2022/23 £20m, 2023/24 £30m, 2024/25 £40m). These recurring overspends have depleted general fund working balances to £66m as at 31 March 2026, equivalent to 4.3% of net budget, below the Council's target of 5-10%. The auditor notes this depletion is not sustainable.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council facing similar social care pressures would need to understand whether this is a persistent management failure or structural underfunding, and what reserve position becomes critical.
findings.figures: £21.6m net overspend in 2025/26 (4th consecutive year); £42.9m ASCH overspend; working balances £66m (4.3% of budget)
findings.quote: 2025/26 marked the fourth consecutive year in which the Council has reported an overspend, notwithstanding the implementation of a range of in-year mitigating actions. These recurring overspends have been funded through the use of general fund working balances, which reduced to £66m as at 31 March 2026, equivalent to 4.3% of the Council's net budget. The continued and unplanned depletion of reserves is not sustainable.

findings.headline: Government announced in September 2026 a review of its July 2026 decision to create four unitary authorities in Kent and Medway in 2028, asking councils to pause implementation work.
findings.detail: In July 2026, Government announced the decision to create four unitary authorities in Kent and Medway in 2028. On 7 September 2026, Government announced a review of that decision and requested impacted councils to cease work on implementing it. The council is continuing to work constructively with Kent and Medway authorities on what activity should pause, continue, or be built upon. The council's new Strategic Statement 'Reforming Kent' was developed for a three-year horizon in anticipation of 2028 restructuring, but this timeline is now uncertain.
findings.matters: A reversal or delay to local government reorganisation plans affects the council's medium-term strategy, organizational decisions, partnership structures, and financial projections. A lender needs to understand whether the council's plans and forecasts remain valid under altered governance scenarios.
findings.figures: July 2026: announcement of decision; 7 September 2026: announcement of review; proposed unitary implementation 2028.
findings.quote: In July 2026, Government announced its decision to create four unitary authorities in Kent and Medway in 2028 through Local Government Reorganisation (LGR). On 7 September 2026, Government announced a review of the decision made, asking impacted councils to cease work on implementing  the decision made in July.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure of £292.563m was £102.989m below budget, with £135.526m re-phased to future years.
findings.detail: Capital spending in 2025/26 was £292.563m against a budget of £395.552m. The underspend of £102.989m comprised £135.526m of re-phasing (moving planned expenditure into 2026/27 and beyond across all services) and £29.710m of real variations where projects did not proceed as planned. Schools directly incurred £12.327m of capital expenditure under devolved arrangements.
findings.matters: Capital re-phasing of this scale—35% of budgeted expenditure—signals material changes to the council's investment delivery plan and affects the timing of cash outflows, borrowing requirements, and medium-term financing needs.
findings.figures: Capital budget £395.552m; outturn £292.563m; underspend £102.989m (re-phasing £135.526m; real variations +£29.710m).
findings.quote: Of this, -£135.526m reflected re-phasing of capital expenditure plans across all services and +£29.710m was due to real variations. Rephased capital resources will be carried forward into 2026/27 and beyond

findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant shows a deficit of £130.5m, driven by high needs budgets overspending by £64.6m in 2025/26, with the council's Safety Valve agreement ended.
findings.detail: The DSG Adjustment Account deficit stands at £130.5m. In 2025/26, the Central DSG Reserve recorded a £61.8m net overspend: £64.6m on high needs budgets, £0.4m on school block spend, and a £3.3m underspend on early years. Schools now hold £57.0m of revenue reserves. The council had been under the Department for Education's Safety Valve process since Summer 2022, which ended 31 March 2026. This is being replaced by a High Needs Sustainability Grant, which is subject to an approved SEND Reform Plan and will be received in Autumn 2026. This future grant has not been recognised in the 2025/26 accounts.
findings.matters: A £130.5m DSG deficit with £64.6m of annual high needs overspend represents a structural mismatch between statutory demand and available funding. The transition from the Safety Valve arrangement to a new funding model creates uncertainty about future funding adequacy and whether the structural deficit can be closed.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £130.5m; 2025/26 net overspend £61.8m (High Needs £64.6m); council contribution £14.6m; Safety Valve funding received £14.2m.
findings.quote: there was a £61.8m net overspend in year on the Central DSG Reserve made up of £64.6m overspend on High Needs budgets... The first phase of this is the High Needs Sustainability Grant which, subject to an approved SEND Reform Plan, will be received in Autumn 2026. As such, the grant income has not been recognised as part of our 2025/26 accounts.

findings.headline: Kent drew down £22.7m from general reserves in 2025/26 to fund a revenue overspend of £21.6m.
findings.detail: The council's revenue outturn showed a net overspend of £21.6m, comprised of £23.8m directorate overspend partially offset by £2.2m favourable funding variance. The directorate overspend was driven by ASCH (£42.869m) and CYPE schools delegated budgets (£32.981m), partially offset by underspends elsewhere. Together with £1.1m of roll-forward requests, the overspend and roll-forwards totalling £22.7m were funded entirely from general reserves.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund recurrent spending shortfalls indicates that revenue financing is insufficient for service delivery. Reserve drawdowns are not sustainable year on year and erode the financial resilience that protects against future shocks.
findings.figures: Net overspend £21.6m; reserves drawdown £22.7m; directorate overspend £23.8m.
findings.quote: The overspend (including roll forwards in 2026/27) have been funded by a £22.7m drawdown from General Reserves.

findings.headline: Adult social care spent £42.869m above budget in 2025/26, overspending the directorate's total budget of £701.596m.
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care directorate outturn was £744.465m against a budget of £701.596m. The narrative explains that the council's budget strategy for 2025/26 was revised after experience in 2024/25, when an outcomes approach with resource envelopes took too long to assess whether spending growth could be managed. The revised strategy for 2025/26 was a hybrid approach, but the core problem—spending growth exceeding available funding—remained acute, particularly in adult social care.
findings.matters: An overspend of this scale (£42.869m is 6.1% of the directorate budget) signals that recurrent spending pressures in adult care cannot be controlled through budget management alone, and will concern any finance director or lender managing similar demographic and inflationary pressures.
findings.figures: Budget £701.596m; outturn £744.465m; overspend £42.869m.
findings.quote: Adult Social Care including Public Health ASCH 701,596  744,465  42,869

findings.paper_title: Kent Pension Fund - Audit Findings Report 2025-26 - Final
findings.headline: 2025 triennial pension valuation completed successfully with member data tested and confirmed accurate; sets employer contribution rates for 2026–2029

findings.matters: Triennial valuations set employer contribution levels and the fund's funding trajectory; successful completion with verified accurate member data supports soundness of contribution rate setting for the next three years

findings.paper_title: Kent Pension Fund - Audit Findings Report 2025-26 - Final
findings.headline: Four control recommendations raised including privileged access issues in Oracle Fusion and Altair pension administration systems
findings.detail: Auditors identified four control recommendations: investment market value changes recorded on manual spreadsheet outside general ledger rather than through system (Green/low risk); two historic pension records on microfiche not readily retrievable (Amber); one Oracle Fusion user with Financial Application Administrator role not required for their duties, since remedied (Amber); Head of Pensions Administration with full Altair CLIENT administrative access not required for role, to be downgraded (Amber).
findings.matters: System access controls and segregation of duties affect fraud risk and data integrity; unresolved access control weaknesses are material to governance assessment and internal control environment

findings.headline: £4.3 million adjustment made to investment assets post-publication of draft financial statements following delayed receipt of fund manager valuations

findings.detail: Kent migrated its financial management system from Oracle EBS to Oracle Fusion in August 2025. Auditors reviewed project governance, testing, and data migration controls. findings.paper_title: Kent County Council 2025-26 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Significant delays in generating complete debtor and creditor listings following Oracle Fusion implementation caused audit delays

Delays were primarily due to user inexperience with the new system. Auditors raised a High-priority recommendation to implement periodic soft closes and routine reconciliations to improve reporting quality and timeliness.
findings.matters: Post-implementation control weaknesses on a material financial system indicate heightened risk of undetected errors in revenue and expenditure accounting during the transition period.
findings.figures: Significant delays and significant balances unable to be substantiated

findings.paper_title: Kent County Council 2025-26 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Pension liability of £39m at 31 March 2026, up from £29m in prior year
findings.detail: The Authority's defined benefit pension liability increased by £10m despite an underlying pension fund surplus of £735m. The increase reflects the asset ceiling restriction under IFRIC 14, which limits recognition of pension assets to the present value of economic benefits available through refunds or contribution reductions. This is a technical accounting treatment but represents a material balance sheet movement.
findings.matters: Pension liability movements and asset ceiling restrictions are material to borrowing capacity and long-term financial planning for councils with defined benefit exposure.
findings.figures: £39m liability at 31 March 2026 (up from £29m at 31 March 2025); underlying fund surplus £735m
findings.quote: The actuarial valuation of Kent Pension Fund at 31 March 2026 showed an overall pension surplus, and hence, the Authority results showed a pension surplus amounting to £735m. IAS 19 and IFRIC 14 require that the pension asset / surplus is limited to the present value of economic benefits available as a refund or lower future contributions as contributions are assumed to continue for the full period of the Authority's participation in the Pension Fund. The application of the asset ceiling means that a pension liability of £39m, reflecting the unfunded deficit element of the scheme, has been recorded at 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Kent County Council 2025-26 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Oracle Cloud Programme budget increased to £43m from £15m approved in 2023
findings.detail: Finance system (phase 1) went live August 2025 with initial operational issues: debtors and creditors reporting was inaccurate, causing significant audit delays due to staff inexperience with the new system. A privileged access control deficiency was also identified. Phase 2 (payroll) is planned for early 2027. The £28m cost overrun (187% increase) reflects scope expansion and lessons from phase 1.
findings.matters: Major capital programme with substantial cost overrun and post-implementation control weaknesses signals governance and budget management risks on transformation activity.
findings.figures: Budget increased from £15m to £43m; phase 1 went live August 2025; phase 2 planned early 2027
findings.quote: The budget for the project has increased since inception in 2023, with a recent report to Cabinet setting out that the project was now expected to cost £43m.

findings.paper_title: Kent County Council 2025-26 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: General Fund balance fell to 4% of net revenue budget, below the Authority's 5-10% policy target
findings.detail: Total useable reserves fell from £252m to £210m in one year. Of the £210m remaining, only £25.5m (12%) is available for general use; £184.5m is earmarked for specific purposes. The Council has drawn down reserves to balance the budget, leaving minimal buffer for unexpected costs or further demand pressure.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is unsustainable as a deficit-funding mechanism; with general reserves at 4% and DSG deficits growing, the council's financial flexibility is critically constrained.
findings.figures: General Fund balance 4% of net revenue budget vs 5-10% target; total useable reserves £209.927m (down from £252.033m); available reserves £25.456m
findings.quote: Of the £210m held in useable reserves, only 12% of that total is available for general use, should there be unplanned and unexpected expenditure that the Authority is required to fund – such as SEND deficits.

findings.paper_title: Kent County Council 2025-26 Audit Findings Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £130.463m in 2025-26, up from £97.483m in prior year
findings.detail: The DSG deficit grew 34% year-on-year despite a Department for Education grant of £162.5m approved to cover 90% of the accumulated deficit. The statutory override preventing impact on general fund balances ends March 2028, creating material uncertainty about how deficits for 2026-27 and 2027-28 will be funded once the override ceases.
findings.matters: SEND spending is pushing councils into structural deficit; the statutory override ends in 21 months, and Kent's deficit growth trajectory suggests general fund impact may be unavoidable regardless of the DfE grant.
findings.figures: £130.463m (2025-26), £97.483m (2024-25), £67.167m (2023-24); £162.5m grant covers 90% of accumulated deficit; statutory override ends March 2028
findings.quote: This override will cease in March 2028. The Authority have submitted a SEND Reform plan to the Department for Education, which has been approved and agrees a £162.5m grant, covering 90% of the existing deficit, with adjustments for safety valve payments. It is currently unclear how the inevitable deficits for 2026-27 and 2027-28 will be funded, and what impact, if any there will be on general fund balances.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Adult Social Care Older People services overspent by £8.9m; residential care unit costs and community support usage above budget.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care & Health directorate shows a net overspend of £9.1m. The primary driver is Older People Residential Care Services at +£6.4m, caused by average placement costs being higher than budget and lower-than-expected income from service user contributions (reflecting lower numbers paying full cost of care). A secondary pressure is Older People Community Based Services at +£2.1m, driven by higher Direct Payments volumes and lower income from client charges. These service lines sit within a long-term support division budgeted at £696.6m.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a large cost base (£786.7m budget, 47% of General Fund) with inelastic demand. Rising unit costs and usage pressures here indicate demographic and social care market pressures that are structural and likely to recur.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care & Health total budget £786.7m, forecast £795.8m (overspend £9.1m or 1.2%). Older People residential care overspend £6.4m, community services overspend £2.1m.
findings.quote: Pressures on this service line relate to the average costs of placements being higher than budgeted for which has been impacted by undeliverable savings, alongside reduced levels of income which is due to a combination of factors including reductions in the number of service users who pay for the full cost of their care.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Adult Social Care and Children's Services forecast to deliver 86-90% of savings targets; strategic service changes slipping.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care forecast to deliver £37.3m of £41.7m savings (89.6%), with £2.0m shortfall due to delayed implementation of a new Older People Residential & Nursing contract planned for Q2/3 rather than Q1. Children, Young People & Education forecast to deliver £18.4m of £21.3m (86.4%), with £0.953m of an invest-to-save in-house residential scheme not landing due to delayed home openings, £0.704m of residential special schools savings unachieved, and £0.601m of legal services efficiencies depending on Court proceedings acceleration.
findings.matters: Large service directorates are not delivering planned savings at the expected pace. Commissioning and strategic transformation milestones (contract mobilizations, new service models, facility openings) are slipping, indicating either over-ambitious targets or constrained delivery capability.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care: £41.7m target, £37.3m forecast (89.6%), £2.0m shortfall. Children, Young People & Education: £21.3m target, £18.4m forecast (86.4%), principal shortfalls £0.953m residential units, £0.704m schools, £0.601m legal.
findings.quote: A new Older People Residential & Nursing (OPRN) contract is planned for Quarter 2/3 which will introduce a new sustainable pricing model. Ahead of implementation ASC are managing cost pressures during the transition period ensuring affordability of all new placements until the new contract is mobilised.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Early debt redemption of £60m in 2025-26 generated £0.683m discount and £2.420m annual interest saving.
findings.detail: The council repaid £50m of debt in September 2025 and £10m in March 2025 ahead of maturity, obtaining a 10-year discount of £0.683m and achieving an annual interest cost saving of £2.420m. This was deliberate treasury strategy to lock in savings at favourable relative rates. However, the report notes that this action reduced cash balances and created short-term borrowing requirements, indicating tight liquidity management.
findings.matters: Early redemption reflects active debt management and sound rate-risk positioning. However, it reduced liquidity headroom and necessitated compensating short-term borrowing, indicating the council is managing cash flow tightly without significant buffer.
findings.figures: Debt redemptions £50m (September 2025) and £10m (March 2025), discount £0.683m, annual interest saving £2.420m.
findings.quote: Annual discount received for 10 years on £50m early debt redemption in September 2025 and £10m in March 2025 ... Impact on debt interest costs of £50m early debt redemption in 2025-26

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: General Fund reserves drawn down by £21.4m to fund in-year overspend; will fall to minimum threshold of 5.1%.
findings.detail: The £21.4m revenue overspend for 2026-27 must be funded from reserves. General Fund reserves are forecast to move from -£66.0m to -£84.8m, representing 5.1% of the net revenue budget (£1,655.6m). This comprises: repayment of previous overspend drawdown (£20.2m), rebuilding contribution (£16.8m), and current year overspend drawdown (£21.4m). The council's stated minimum target is 5% of net revenue budget.
findings.matters: Drawing down reserves to fund operational overspend weakens financial resilience and increases future replenishment requirements. At the minimum threshold with no buffer, any further adverse variance will cause the reserve to fall below policy minimum.
findings.figures: General Fund reserve opening balance -£66.0m, forecast closing -£84.8m (5.1% of £1,655.6m net revenue budget), in-year overspend funded from reserves £21.4m.
findings.quote: When the council overspends, it must fund that overspend from reserves. Any overspend is a concern for the authority and presents a risk to the Council's future financial sustainability and it is essential that the need to drawdown from reserves is reduced as far as possible, as drawdowns from reserves weaken the Council's financial resilience and increase the requirement to replenish reserves in future years.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: £4.1m of planned savings for 2026-27 are undeliverable; £5.1m delayed to future years.
findings.detail: Of the £91.7m gross savings target for 2026-27, the council forecasts delivery of only £82.5m (90%). Of the £9.2m shortfall, £4.1m is identified as undeliverable (will not be achieved). Key undeliverable items: £2.0m Adult Social Care commissioning (new contract mobilization delayed to Q2/3), £0.7m legal savings (dependent on Courts speeding up proceedings, deemed unlikely), £0.6m contingent on Government actions on residential care costs. A further £5.1m of planned savings will now be delivered in future years instead.
findings.matters: Undeliverable savings indicate structural overspend: the underlying cost base is higher than planned. Savings targets of this scale not materializing suggest either the plans were over-ambitious or delivery capability is constrained. This implies future-year budgets face similar slippage risk.
findings.figures: Savings target £91.7m, forecast delivery £82.5m (90%), undeliverable £4.1m, delayed to future years £5.1m.
findings.quote: As at Quarter 1, £82.5m is expected to be delivered in 2026-27, which represents 90% delivery against the target. £9.2m of savings are currently not expected to be delivered in 2026-27. Of this amount, £5.1m is planned to be delivered in future financial years, with the remaining £4.1m no longer deliverable.

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Looked After Children numbers rising 5% (70 more children); residential care costs up 23% year-on-year.
findings.detail: The number of Looked After Children has increased by 70 (5%) in the past year, with cost pressures driven by a shift from in-house foster care (declining capacity) to more expensive external market placements. Residential care costs have risen 23% between March 2025 and March 2026. This is generating a permanent forecast overspend of £16.8m for 2026-27, with a further £2.5m contingency for possible additional increases in numbers and costs. Mitigation through opening of four new in-house residential homes is slipping, with two homes now due to open later than planned, reducing expected savings by nearly £1m.
findings.matters: Demand-driven and cost-pressured. A 5% volume increase plus 23% price inflation on a service that is difficult to control represents structural, recurring financial pressure. The forecast shows mitigation plans slipping, with no certainty of future cost stabilization.
findings.figures: 70 additional LAC (5% year-on-year increase), residential care costs increased 23% between March 2025 and March 2026, forecast overspend £16.8m plus £2.5m contingency.
findings.quote: Historically the number of Looked After Children (LAC) has remained relatively steady but the number has started to rise since the last quarter of 2025-26, with 70 more children than a year ago (5% increase).

findings.paper_title: 26-00055 - Revenue and Capital Budget Forecast Outturn Report – Quarter 1, 2026-2027
findings.headline: Schools DSG deficit forecast to increase to £238.5m; £162.5m government grant depends on DfE approval of reform plan not yet received.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to increase from £130.5m to £238.5m in 2026-27. This is dependent on approval of a High Needs Stability Grant of £162.5m, which the council applied for in June 2026 and has not yet received. The statutory override allowing councils to hold DSG deficits separate from general reserves expires 31 March 2028. From 2028-29 onwards, the government has only stated an intention (not a guarantee) that councils will not be required to fund DSG deficits from the General Fund.
findings.matters: A £238.5m DSG deficit is a material financial liability. The funding solution depends entirely on government approval of an outcome still being determined. Once the statutory override ends in 15 months, the council faces funding uncertainty for the remaining deficit.
findings.figures: DSG deficit forecast £238.5m (from £130.5m opening), High Needs Stability Grant expected £162.5m (not approved), High Needs Block in-year overspend £109.2m, statutory override expires 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: This forecast position does not include the impact of the new High Needs Stability Grant, announced in February 2026, which depends on the Department for Education (DfE) approving a local Special Educational Needs & Disability (SEND) reform plan.

findings.headline: Information Commissioner's Office monitoring KCC performance on data subject access requests, with compliance at 57% vs 90% target
findings.detail: Subject Access Request (SAR) compliance was 57% (target 90%, floor 85%) — RED. The report states "The Information Commissioner's Office continues to monitor KCC's performance." 77% of requests come from the Children, Young People and Education Directorate, with SEN the main source of overdue cases. Performance declined for the second quarter in a row but is similar to the same quarter last year.
findings.matters: ICO monitoring is a formal compliance risk. Sustained non-compliance with statutory data protection timescales creates legal and reputational exposure. The concentration in SEN suggests EHCP-related cases are driving the backlog.
findings.figures: 57% within timescale vs 90% target (floor 85%); 77% of requests from CYPE; majority overdue relate to SEN.
findings.quote: For Subject Access Requests (SARs), performance decreased for the second quarter in a row, but is similar to the same quarter last year... The Information Commissioner's Office continues to monitor KCC's performance.

findings.headline: NHS Health Checks delivery fell to 4,677 in Q1 against 31,000 target, a 20% drop from previous quarter, due to provider transition
findings.detail: Only 4,677 NHS Health Checks were delivered in Q1 against a target of 31,000 (15% of target; floor 24,800). This represents a 20% drop from the previous quarter (5,831). The report attributes the failure to "service changes, including the transition to new provider arrangements." No forward recovery plan is outlined. This is a mandated public health function.
findings.matters: A 74% miss against target on a preventive health programme suggests the provider transition was poorly managed or under-resourced. The scale of the shortfall indicates either service capacity was overstated or transition planning was inadequate.
findings.figures: 4,677 delivered vs 31,000 target (15% achievement); 24,800 floor; down from 5,831 previous quarter (20% decline).
findings.quote: Delivery of NHS Health Checks was significantly affected during this quarter by a number of service changes, including the transition to new provider arrangements.

findings.headline: Border resilience risk escalated to High on confirmation that EU and France will not pause checks, with infrastructure implications
findings.detail: Corporate Risk CRR0042 (Border fluidity, infrastructure and resilience) was escalated from Medium (15) to High (20) on 16 July 2026. The escalation followed "confirmation being received from the EU and France that there is no flexibility in temporarily pausing border checks." The implications for Kent, given Dover's position as England's primary freight gateway and Sevington Inland Border Facility throughput, include sustained congestion pressure, potential revenue impact on transport/parking services, and ongoing operational strain on council-coordinated responses.
findings.matters: A formal risk escalation affecting a strategic asset (Kent's border infrastructure) signals the council now faces sustained operational pressure in this area with no policy relief available. This can create unfunded cost pressures and affect revenue streams from services dependent on fluid border movement.
findings.figures: Risk escalation: Medium (score 15) to High (score 20); confirmed on 16/07/2026; no flexibility available from EU/France.
findings.quote: RISK RATING INCREASED: CRR0042 Border fluidity, infrastructure and resilience – Increased on 16/07/26 from Medium (15) to High (20) due to confirmation being received from the EU and France that there is no flexibility in temporarily pausing border checks.

findings.headline: Procurement 'savings' of £32.9m claimed but 75% are non-cashable cost avoidance, mostly from one-off highways contract
findings.detail: The council reports £32.9m in financial benefits, with £23.5m (71.5%) from the new Highway Term Maintenance Contract. However, the report explicitly states "the majority of financial benefits are categorised as cost avoidance, totalling £24.73m. This reflects the role of procurement activity in avoiding higher costs through effective tendering... However, these financial benefits should be distinguished from immediate cashable budget reductions." The £8m HTMC saving came from negotiation reducing tendered rates by 22%. The report cautions this is "exceptional" performance and the quarter "should be treated as exceptional reporting rather than requiring an adjustment of targets."
findings.matters: A headline 'savings' figure of £32.9m cannot be used to offset overspends or released to the budget — 75% is unrealised cost avoidance. The one-off nature and contractor-specific scale makes it unavailable for forward financial planning.
findings.figures: £32.9m total; £23.5m HTMC (71%); £24.73m cost avoidance (75%); HTMC delivery includes £8m negotiation on initial tender.
findings.quote: The majority of financial benefits are categorised as cost avoidance, totalling £24.73m. This reflects the role of procurement activity in avoiding higher costs through effective tendering, negotiation and challenge of pricing. However, these financial benefits should be distinguished from immediate cashable budget reductions. As a result, the quarter should be treated as exceptional reporting quarter, rather than requiring an adjustment of targets.

findings.headline: Developer contributions at highest level in 32 months, bringing £71.4m of capital funding for growth infrastructure
findings.detail: S106 contributions secured totalled £71.4m in Q1, representing 99.97% of amounts sought and the highest figure since December 2023. Contributions were concentrated in two major Thanet developments: £40.3m from a 1,600-dwelling scheme at Birchington (including £20.95m highways, £18.67m education) and £28.2m from 1,461-dwelling scheme at Margate (£19.63m education, £7.98m highways). The council achieved a 99.97% success rate against originally requested amounts.
findings.matters: Substantial incoming capital funding locked in for council infrastructure investment. A funding source that is predictable and now demonstrating strong collection suggests the council's ability to deliver growth-related capital schemes without increasing borrowing.
findings.figures: £71.4m total; £40.3m Birchington (1,600 dwellings); £28.2m Margate (1,461 dwellings); 99.97% success rate against amounts sought.
findings.quote: A total of £71.4m in contributions was secured this quarter, representing the highest figure since December 2023. This significant increase is largely attributable to two strategic developments granted planning permission in the Thanet district.

findings.headline: Emergency highways response fell to 73% of target following May 2026 transition to Ringway, with data system configuration issues under investigation
findings.detail: Following transition to Ringway as the new Highway Term Maintenance Contract (HTMC) provider in May 2026, emergency incident response fell to 73% of target (89% in April under previous provider Amey). The report states: "Issues have been identified with the reporting systems and the configuration of data transfers between systems, which are affecting the accuracy of performance reporting. As a result, the underlying data and reporting outputs are currently being jointly investigated by KCC and Ringway." Routine enquiry response is also RED at 73%.
findings.matters: A major outsourced service shows both operational failure (emergency response) and data integrity failure (unable to reliably report performance). Both create immediate service risk and prevent accurate monitoring of contractor delivery.
findings.figures: Emergency incidents: 73% actual vs 98% target (floor 95%); April performance under Amey: 89%; routine enquiries: 73% vs 90% target.
findings.quote: Issues have been identified with the reporting systems and the configuration of data transfers between systems, which are affecting the accuracy of performance reporting. As a result, the underlying data and reporting outputs are currently being jointly investigated by KCC and Ringway to establish an agreed and validated performance position, to ensure accurate reporting of data.

findings.headline: Children's services staffing fell 5.2 percentage points in quarter, dropping to 82.6% of target and increasing reliance on agency spend
findings.detail: Percentage of the case-holding establishment with staff in post fell from 87.8% to 82.6%, a decline of 5.2pp and below the 90% target. This is the second consecutive quarter of decline and sits just 2.6pp above the 80% floor. The report does not provide forward staffing plans.
findings.matters: Persistent staffing shortfalls typically drive higher-cost agency engagement, increase service quality risk, and create budget volatility. A 5.2pp quarterly drop signals deteriorating recruitment or retention.
findings.figures: 82.6% current vs 87.8% previous quarter; 2.4pp above floor of 80%; target 90%.
findings.quote: Percentage of the case-holding establishment with a member of staff present in post AMBER. Latest: 82.6% Target: 90%, Floor 80% Previous: 87.8%

findings.headline: Safeguarding caseload at highest level in 18 months, signalling rising demand and forward cost pressure
findings.detail: Open safeguarding work increased from 2,418 to 2,881 in Quarter 1, described as "highest level since Quarter 3, 2024/25." This tracks a pattern of rising incoming concerns: 6,029 received this quarter, up from 5,796 in the previous quarter. The report attributes some increase to "hot weather" but notes the broader trend has been upward.
findings.matters: Growing safeguarding caseload creates forward pressure on staffing budgets and service costs. Unmet caseload growth is an early warning of future spending needs or service quality deterioration.
findings.figures: 2,881 open cases; up from 2,418 previous quarter (19% increase); up from lowest level of 2,418 in Quarter 4 2024/25; 6,029 concerns received vs 5,796 previous quarter.
findings.quote: Open work is at its highest level since Quarter 3, 2024/25. In Quarter 1, the amount of open work increased from 2,418 to 2,881, this will be a mixture of ongoing enquiries and incoming concerns that are being triaged.

findings.headline: Adult social care residential admissions now exceed a newly lowered target, signalling demand pressure despite tightened expectations
findings.detail: Admissions to residential and nursing care for adults aged 65+ reached 576 per 100,000 (rolling 12-month), measured against a new target of 515 — down from 588 in the previous year. Despite the lower threshold, performance is RED. The report notes "the target for this measure has changed for this financial year" and is "based on performance in 2024/25," indicating the council set a tighter benchmark it has failed to meet.
findings.matters: The council has explicitly tightened its admission target yet still overshot it. This signals underlying demand pressures that the authority cannot contain and suggests structural spending above its own revised tolerance.
findings.figures: 576 actual vs 515 target (floor 560); change from 588 to 515 target year-on-year represents a 12% reduction in acceptable admissions but actual performance did not improve.
findings.quote: Long Term support needs of older people (65 and over) met by admission to residential and nursing care homes, per 100,000 – rolling 12 months. Latest: 576 Target: 515, Floor: 560 Previous: 584 (Green). The target for this measure has changed for this financial year, moving from 588 to 515.

findings.headline: SEND placement costs rising as new special schools remain delayed, forcing greater reliance on expensive independent provision
findings.detail: 10.8% of pupils with EHCPs are placed in independent or out-of-county special schools against a target of 9%. The report attributes this to "delayed provision of two new special schools, leading to a continued over-reliance on independent specialist provision to compensate." Despite recent DfE assurance that the schools remain in their plans, the report states this "is likely to remain below target for the foreseeable future."
findings.matters: Direct and ongoing budget pressure: independent school fees are substantially higher than maintained provision. Delayed capital delivery is forcing sustained overspend on recurrent costs.
findings.figures: 10.8% vs target 9.0%; KCC is 0.8 percentage points above tolerance and acknowledges ongoing pressure from new school approvals in the independent sector.
findings.quote: The percentage of pupils with EHCPs being placed in independent or out of county special schools, at 10.8%, remains higher than the target of 9.0%. As previously reported, Kent continues to feel the effect of the delayed provision of two new special schools, leading to a continued over-reliance on independent specialist provision to compensate.

findings.headline: Capital spending includes a £35.2m rephasing variance, indicating project deferrals.
findings.detail: The capital forecast outturn shows a £32m total underspend split between a £3.1m real underspend and a -£35.2m rephasing variance. The significant rephasing element indicates £35.2m of budgeted capital projects are being deferred into future financial years.
findings.matters: Large capital rephasing affects the council's multi-year borrowing requirements and may indicate delivery constraints or scheme viability concerns that affect capital programme credibility.
findings.figures: £32m underspend; £3.1m real variance; -£35.2m rephasing variance
findings.quote: The capital forecast outturn position is a £32m underspend against budget, split between a £3.1m real variance and a -£35.2m rephasing variance.

findings.headline: Kent is forecasting a £21.4m revenue overspend in 2026-27, representing 1.3% of the overall budget.
findings.detail: In Q1 monitoring, the Council reports a revenue forecast outturn variance of £21.4m overspend against budget. This indicates the Council is running ahead of budget in the opening quarter of the financial year, requiring either corrective action or explanation of how the overspend will be managed.
findings.matters: A material Q1 overspend suggests the council may struggle to deliver its full-year budget and raises questions about spend control and reserves sustainability.
findings.figures: £21.4m overspend; 1.3% of overall budget
findings.quote: The forecast outturn variance against the revenue budget is an overspend of £21.4m, which represents 1.3% of the overall budget.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Fund administration faces staffing shortages affecting operational capacity.
findings.detail: Administration staffing was underspent (budget £3.455m, actual £3.382m) not through cost control but because vacancies were unfilled or filled from internal candidates, leaving 'backfill vacancies outstanding'. This indicates recruitment and retention challenges within the administration team.
findings.matters: Understaffing in pension administration increases operational risk, processing delays, and error potential; combined with the data quality issues reported separately, it suggests the team is under resource pressure.
findings.figures: Administration staffing budget: £3.455m; actual: £3.382m (underspent £73k)
findings.quote: Administration staffing costs had an underspend due to the budget being set anticipating vacancies being filled. However, where recruitment campaigns have been completed and vacancies filled, some have come from internal candidates which leave backfill vacancies outstanding.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Pension data rectification project faces delays due to system access issues.
findings.detail: The multi-year data rectification project, budgeted at £2.012m, incurred only £1.020m in 2025-26. The underspend reflects delays rather than savings: 'Progress has been impacted by issues relating to system access and ensuring accurate data has been received from employers.' The project is required for Pensions Dashboard compliance.
findings.matters: Data quality problems in pension administration suggest underlying IT or operational weaknesses; failure to complete the project and meet the Dashboard deadline could result in regulatory penalties.
findings.figures: Data rectification project budget £2.012m; actual spend £1.020m; shortfall £991k
findings.quote: The data rectification project is a multi-year exercise and is progressing, but the invoicing is dependent on progress being made. Progress has been impacted by issues relating to system access and ensuring accurate data has been received from employers.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation poses unprecedented structural risk to the fund.
findings.detail: The Fund Chairman identifies LGR as 'one of the most consequential developments facing the Fund', noting it will have 'important implications for governance, employer participation, administration and member services'. The Fund is engaged in cross-authority project work to assess impact and determine future host authority arrangements, but outcomes remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Major local government reorganisation could reshape the fund's employer base, governance structure, and financial position; this represents material risk to both Kent County Council and its credit position.
findings.figures: 265 active employers (down from 272 in prior year); 185,028 total fund members
findings.quote: Looking ahead, one of the most consequential developments facing the Fund is Local Government Reorganisation. The scale of change proposed across local government is unprecedented and will have important implications for governance, employer participation, administration and member services.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Fund assets increased by almost £1bn to £9.4bn, driven by strong investment returns.
findings.detail: Net fund assets grew from £8.451bn to £9.418bn, an increase of £966.7m. Investment performance delivered 11.5% return, outperforming the benchmark of 10.8%, occurring despite pausing certain asset transitions pending completion of the move to Border to Coast Pensions Partnership.
findings.matters: A growing fund improves the council's pension position, reduces the risk of future contribution increases, and indicates effective investment management through a period of governance transition.
findings.figures: Fund value 2024-25: £8.451bn; 2025-26: £9.418bn; increase £966.7m; investment return 11.5% vs benchmark 10.8%
findings.quote: Investment assets have continued to grow in value in a supportive investment environment, taking the Fund from £8.45bn in 2024/25, to £9.42bn in 2025/26, an increase of almost £1bn.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Fund management and administration costs jumped 39% in one year.
findings.detail: Total costs (administration, governance, and investment management) increased from £40.1m to £55.8m, a jump of £15.7m. Fund manager fees alone increased approximately £2.5m due to higher asset valuations and fee structures; additional significant costs came from property acquisition transactions undertaken to rebalance the portfolio.
findings.matters: Rapidly escalating administrative costs reduce the net benefit to the fund and employers; a lender would want to understand whether this cost inflation is permanent and sustainable.
findings.quote: Fund manager fees have increased by roughly £2.5m when compared to the budget. This is as a result of forecasts being set on estimate valuations set 12 months in advance. In this case, those valuations had grown at a quicker pace than forecast, especially in the equities asset class which is very volatile. As fees are paid on the value of asset under management, this has led to an increase in fees.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Pension benefit payments are growing much faster than contribution income.
findings.detail: Annual benefit payments increased 6.3% in the year to £353.5m, outpacing contribution growth. Over five years, benefits have grown 37% while pensioner numbers have risen 18%, showing the fund is in a paying-out phase with more retirees and fewer working members proportionally.
findings.matters: Although the fund is currently 104% funded, this structural imbalance means long-term sustainability depends on sustained investment returns; a significant market downturn could quickly reverse the surplus and force higher employer contributions.
findings.quote: The amount the Fund spends on benefits has increased by 6.3% over the year, which was slightly above the increase in contribution income, and by 37% since 2021/22.

findings.paper_title: 11 (a) - Appendix One - Kent Pension Fund Annual Report and Accounts
findings.headline: Pension fund improved to 104% funded; employers will pay lower contribution rates.
findings.detail: The triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 shows the fund's funding level improved from 102% to 104%. This improvement resulted in lower contribution rates for the majority of participating employers, explicitly described as 'particularly welcome at a time when many local authorities and public sector bodies continue to face significant financial challenges'.
findings.matters: Lower pension contribution rates ease pressure on the council's revenue budget at a time of financial strain; this improves the council's ability to fund other services and remain solvent.
findings.figures: Funding level: 102% (2025 valuation) to 104% (2026 valuation); contribution rates lower for majority of employers
findings.quote: the valuation resulted in lower contribution rates for the majority of participating employers. This was particularly welcome at a time when many local authorities and public sector bodies continue to face significant financial challenges.

findings.headline: Pension aggregation case processing KPI fell from 75% in April to 32.3% in June, declining 43 percentage points over two months
findings.detail: Aggregation actual cases KPI performance declined from 75% in April to 32.3% in June, a 43-percentage-point drop over two months. The intermediate May figure of 64.7% suggests consistent deterioration through the quarter.
findings.matters: Significant declines in pension processing KPIs could indicate capacity shortages, control failures, or systemic issues that might delay member benefits and trigger regulatory concerns.
findings.figures: Aggregation actuals KPI: April 75%, May 64.7%, June 32.3%
findings.quote: Aggregation actuals 4 75 17 64.7 62 32.3

findings.headline: Pension scheme data quality improved from below to above regulatory compliance standard
findings.detail: Scheme-specific data quality as measured by TPR (The Pensions Regulator) pass rate improved from 83.15% in Q4 2025-26 to 97.95% in Q2 2026. This indicates resolution of a regulatory data quality issue that had previously been below acceptable compliance levels.
findings.matters: Regulatory data quality compliance is a prerequisite for unqualified pension scheme operation; movement from below-compliance to compliance indicates remediation of a governance weakness.
findings.figures: Scheme Specific TPR Pass Rate: 83.15% (Jan-Mar 2026) to 97.95% (Apr-Jun 2026)
findings.quote: Scheme Specific 83.15 97.95

findings.headline: Administration staff budget running £155,098 under budget while most other cost lines overspend.
findings.detail: Against a budgeted administration payroll of £4,296,332, the forecast shows spend of only £4,141,234. This is the largest single saving in the forecast and partially offsets widespread overspends elsewhere. The underspend may indicate staff vacancies or turnover not yet filled.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand whether staffing savings are planned or incidental to their forecasting, as sustained vacancies can either represent genuine savings or risk to service delivery and future recruitment costs.
findings.figures: Administration Staff budget £4,296,332; forecast £4,141,234; underspend £155,098
findings.quote: Administration Staff 4,296,332 4,141,234 155,098

findings.headline: Pension fund administration forecast shows £233,260 overspend in Q1, with staff underspend offset by operational cost overruns.
findings.detail: The Q1 forecast projects total administration costs of £59,647,422 against a budget of £59,414,162. A £155,098 underspend in administration staff is more than offset by overspends across multiple operational areas: IT expenses £152,644 over budget, printing and mailing costs £69,648 over, KCC overhead recharges £50,902 over, and pooling costs £37,900 over, among others.
